title: Splints, Wounds & Bedside Procedures
summary: The hands-on half of the ED tech job: building splints that hold, cleaning wounds so they do not get infected, setting up trays, and assisting the procedures that happen at the bedside every shift.

lessons.title: Splinting principles and the check that protects the limb
lessons.body:
## Why immobilizing helps

A fracture hurts because the broken ends grind against the bone's nerve-rich outer wrapper (periosteum) and tear into muscle every time the limb moves. Hold the pieces still and you cut the pain, slow the bleeding into the tissue, and keep a sharp bone end from cutting an artery or nerve. That is the whole job of a splint: stop motion, protect what is still intact.

A splint only stops motion if it controls the joint above and the joint below the injury. Leave the elbow free on a forearm splint and the two forearm bones still rotate against each other every time the patient turns a doorknob.

## The rules that never change

1. Immobilize the joint above and the joint below the fracture.
2. Pad every bony bump: wrist bones, elbow, ankle bones, heel, the head of the fibula. Skin squeezed over bone for a few hours becomes a pressure sore.
3. Splint in the position of function unless the provider orders otherwise. For the hand that is the wrist extended `20-30 degrees`, knuckles (MCP joints) bent `70-90 degrees`, the finger joints nearly straight, and the thumb held out as if wrapped around a soda can.
4. Nothing rigid goes all the way around a fresh injury. Plaster or fiberglass wrapped a full 360 degrees is a cast, and a cast on a limb that is still swelling is how compartment syndrome starts. A splint is rigid on one or two sides and elastic on the rest, so swelling has somewhere to go.
5. Ice `20 minutes` at a time over the splint and keep the limb above the level of the heart.
6. Run your hand over the finished splint hunting for ridges, wrinkles and hard edges. Every one of them is a future pressure point.

## Circulation, motor, sensation: before and after

The neurovascular check is three separate findings, and you document all three with a time, once before the splint goes on and once after it is wrapped.

- **Circulation** is the pulse past the injury (radial at the wrist, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial at the foot), plus skin color, warmth, and capillary refill under `2 seconds`.
- **Motor** is movement that does not require moving the fracture: wiggle and spread the fingers, bend and straighten the toes.
- **Sensation** is light touch on both sides of each finger or toe, asking the patient whether it feels the same as the other side.

If a pulse or sensation was present before and is gone after, the wrap is too tight. Unwrap it and tell the nurse or provider immediately. Do not wait to see whether it improves on its own.

> **Key:** A splint applied perfectly can still become dangerous in twenty minutes. The post-application check is the safety net, not paperwork.

> **Trap:** "Pulse present" is not a neurovascular check. A patient can have a strong radial pulse and a badly compressed median nerve at the same time.

## What the patient has to hear before they leave

Elevate above the heart, especially for the first `48 hours`. Keep it dry. Do not push anything down inside to scratch.

Come back now, not tomorrow, for numbness or pins-and-needles that will not go away with elevation, for fingers or toes that turn white, blue or cold, for pain that keeps climbing instead of easing, and for pain out of proportion to the injury, especially pain when someone gently straightens the fingers or toes. That last one is the classic early sign of compartment syndrome, and it shows up before the pulse ever disappears.
keyPoints: Immobilize the joint above and the joint below, or the splint does not actually stop motion.
Circulation, motor and sensation are checked and documented before AND after every splint.
Nothing rigid goes fully around a fresh injury; swelling needs somewhere to go.
Hand position of function: wrist extended 20-30 degrees, MCPs bent 70-90 degrees, thumb abducted.
Return precautions: numbness, color change, cold, pain out of proportion or on passive stretch.

checks.q: A patient with a mid-forearm fracture is splinted from the wrist to just below the elbow. What is wrong with this?
choices: Nothing, that covers the fracture
It does not cross the elbow, so the forearm can still rotate
It should have been circumferential plaster
The wrist should have been left free
checks.why: A splint must cross the joint above and below. Leaving the elbow free lets the radius and ulna supinate and pronate against the fracture. Circumferential plaster on a fresh injury is unsafe, and the wrist is the joint below, so it must be included.

checks.q: After you wrap a splint, the patient says two fingers now feel numb. What do you do?
choices: Document it and recheck in an hour
Elevate the arm and reassure the patient
Loosen or remove the wrap now and tell the nurse or provider
Add ice over the splint
checks.why: New numbness after wrapping means the wrap is too tight. It is undone immediately and escalated. Waiting an hour, elevating alone, or adding ice all delay the one action that fixes the problem.

checks.q: Which finding worries you most for early compartment syndrome in a splinted forearm?
choices: Pain that is severe when someone gently straightens the fingers
A capillary refill of 2 seconds
Mild swelling of the fingers
Absent radial pulse as the first sign
checks.why: Pain out of proportion, especially on passive stretch, is the earliest reliable sign. Capillary refill under 2 seconds is normal, mild swelling is expected, and a lost pulse is a very late finding, not an early one.

lessons.title: Materials and how a splint is actually built
lessons.body:
## Three materials, three trade-offs

**Plaster of Paris** is cheap, molds beautifully into the hollows around bone, and sets slowly enough that you have time to shape it. It is heavy, messy, and weaker than fiberglass.

**Fiberglass roll** is light and strong and hardens in `3-5 minutes`, but it is stiffer to mold and the cut edges are sharp until they are padded.

**Prepadded fiberglass** (OCL, Ortho-Glass) is a fiberglass core already sandwiched inside its own padding. You measure and cut it dry, dip it, and lay it on. It is the fastest option and what most busy departments reach for first. You still put stockinette underneath and fold the ends back over the edges.

## Layers, water temperature, and the burn

| Splint location | Plaster layers |
|---|---|
| Upper extremity | 8-10 |
| Lower extremity | 12-15 |

More layers is not stronger in any way that helps the patient. Plaster sets by a chemical reaction that gives off heat (exothermic), so the thicker the stack and the hotter the dip water, the hotter the splint gets against skin. Real full-thickness burns have been caused by plaster splints.

Three things drive that risk: water hotter than body temperature, stacking more than about `20` layers, and insulating the splint while it cures. Use **warm, not hot** water, roughly `20-25 degrees C`. Never lay a setting splint down on a pillow or blanket, because the padding traps the heat right against the patient.

Setting times change what you tell the patient. Plaster stays workable for `2-4 minutes`, is firm at `10-15 minutes`, and does not reach full strength for `24 hours`, so there is no weight bearing on a leg splint for a full day. Fiberglass is rigid in `3-5 minutes` and near full strength in about `30 minutes`.

## The build, in order

1. **Stockinette.** Cut it about `10 cm` longer than the splint at each end so you can fold it back over the raw edges at the finish.
2. **Padding.** Roll Webril from distal to proximal, each turn covering half of the last, `2-3 layers` thick, with an extra layer over bony points and `2` extra turns at each end.
3. **Measure on the good side.** Lay the splint material against the uninjured limb to get your length. Measuring on the injured side means moving the fracture.
4. **Dip and squeeze.** Submerge until the bubbling stops, then squeeze gently along the length. Do not wring plaster out. Press the layers together so they laminate into one slab.
5. **Apply and smooth.** Lay it on the padding and smooth out every ridge with flat hands. Ridges become pressure sores.
6. **Fold the ends back.** Stockinette and padding come down over the sharp ends of the splint material.
7. **ACE wrap distal to proximal**, snug and even, half-overlapping each turn, no creases and no full-tension stretch. Wrapping toward the heart pushes swelling out of the hand. Wrapping the other direction traps it there.
8. **Mold and hold.** Shape it with flat palms while it sets and hold the position until it is firm. Fingertips leave divots, and divots become pressure sores.

> **Key:** Warm water, the right number of layers, and nothing insulating a curing splint. Those three things prevent the burn.

> **On shift:** Have everything cut, the ACE unrolled and the patient positioned before you dip. Once plaster is wet you have about three minutes, and you cannot pause to go hunting for scissors.

> **Trap:** An ACE wrap applied proximal to distal, or stretched to full tension, turns a good splint into a tourniquet.
keyPoints: Plaster: 8-10 layers upper extremity, 12-15 lower extremity.
Warm water at roughly 20-25 degrees C, never hot, and never insulate a curing splint.
Order: stockinette, Webril distal to proximal, splint material, fold ends, ACE distal to proximal.
Measure the splint against the uninjured limb, not the injured one.
Mold with palms, never fingertips, and hold until firm.

checks.q: Why is hot dip water dangerous when applying a plaster splint?
choices: It makes the plaster too weak
Plaster cures exothermically, and hot water plus thick layers can burn the skin
It washes the calcium out of the plaster
It makes the splint take much longer to set
checks.why: The set is a heat-releasing reaction. Hot water accelerates it and adds to the heat load, which combined with thick layers and insulation causes real burns. Hot water actually speeds setting, and it does not weaken or dissolve the material.

checks.q: Which direction is the elastic bandage applied over a finished forearm splint?
choices: Elbow toward the hand, so it lies flat
Hand toward the elbow, half-overlapping each turn
In figure-eights starting at the mid-forearm
Any direction, as long as it is tight
checks.why: Distal to proximal moves swelling toward the heart. Starting at the elbow traps fluid in the hand, and maximum tightness in any direction risks compressing the limb.

lessons.title: Upper extremity splints, one by one
lessons.body:
## Match the splint to the bone

| Injury | Splint | What it must cross |
|---|---|---|
| Distal radius or ulna fracture | Sugar-tong forearm | Wrist and elbow, to block rotation |
| Wrist sprain, carpal fracture, soft tissue | Volar or dorsal forearm | Wrist only |
| Scaphoid fracture or suspicion, thumb UCL tear | Thumb spica | Wrist and thumb |
| 4th or 5th metacarpal (boxer's), proximal phalanx | Ulnar gutter | Wrist through the ring and little fingers |
| 2nd or 3rd metacarpal | Radial gutter | Same, index and middle, with a hole cut for the thumb |
| Elbow or proximal forearm fracture | Posterior long-arm | Elbow at `90 degrees` |
| Humeral shaft fracture | Coaptation plus sling and swathe | Shoulder around the elbow, U-shaped |

## The four you will build most

**Sugar-tong.** One long U-shaped strip that starts at the knuckles on the palm side, runs up the forearm, wraps around the elbow held at `90 degrees`, and comes back down the back of the forearm to the knuckles. Measure it on the good arm first; it usually runs `75-90 cm` in an adult. Forearm neutral with the thumb up, wrist in slight extension, and the material stopped short of the MCP joints on the palm side so the knuckles can still bend. It exists for exactly one reason: a distal radius fracture rotates, and only a splint that crosses the elbow stops supination and pronation.

**Volar or dorsal forearm.** A flat slab running from just below the elbow crease to the palmar crease on the front, or to the knuckles on the back, with the wrist in `20-30 degrees` of extension. Fast and comfortable, and wrong for anything that needs rotation controlled.

**Thumb spica.** A slab that runs along the thumb side of the forearm, over the wrist, and out to the tip of the thumb, holding that soda-can position. It goes on a snuffbox-tender wrist even when the X-ray is normal, because a scaphoid fracture often does not show on film for `10-14 days` and a missed one loses its blood supply and dies (avascular necrosis).

**Ulnar gutter.** A slab folded along the little-finger side of the hand and forearm, covering the ring and little fingers, with padding placed between the fingers so skin does not sit on skin. Position of function again: wrist extended about `20 degrees`, MCPs bent `70-90 degrees`, finger joints nearly straight. A boxer's fracture splinted with straight knuckles stiffens in that position and the patient loses grip.

## Elbow, humerus, fingers and slings

A **posterior long-arm splint** runs from the armpit down the back of the arm, around the elbow at `90 degrees`, and out along the ulnar forearm to the wrist. A **coaptation splint** for a humeral shaft fracture is a U that goes up the inside of the arm, around the elbow, and over the shoulder, letting gravity pull the fracture into alignment; it always gets a sling and swathe with it.

Finger splints are aluminum-foam, molded to rest the injured joint, and taped so the fingertip stays visible for color checks. **Buddy taping** the injured finger to its neighbor, with gauze between to keep the skin dry, works for stable sprains and non-displaced phalanx fractures and lets the finger keep moving.

A **sling** carries the weight of the forearm. A **swathe** is the strap around the chest that stops the arm swinging. Shoulder and humerus injuries need both. Fit the sling so the hand sits slightly higher than the elbow, pad the knot and move it off the spine of the neck, and leave the fingertips out where you can see them.

> **Trap:** A volar splint on a distal radius fracture feels fine to the patient and fails, because it does not cross the elbow and the fracture keeps rotating.

> **On the exam:** Snuffbox tenderness with a normal X-ray still gets a thumb spica and orthopedic follow-up. It is the single most tested splinting decision.
keyPoints: Distal radius fracture gets a sugar-tong, because only crossing the elbow blocks rotation.
Snuffbox tenderness gets a thumb spica even with a normal X-ray; scaphoid fractures hide for 10-14 days.
Boxer's fracture (4th/5th metacarpal) gets an ulnar gutter with MCPs bent 70-90 degrees.
Humeral shaft gets a coaptation splint plus sling and swathe.
Buddy taping keeps a stable finger injury moving; put gauze between the fingers.

checks.q: A 34-year-old falls on an outstretched hand and X-ray shows a distal radius fracture. Which splint does the provider most likely want?
choices: Volar forearm splint
Ulnar gutter
Sugar-tong forearm splint
Thumb spica
checks.why: Sugar-tong crosses the elbow and stops forearm rotation, which a distal radius fracture needs. A volar splint does not cross the elbow, an ulnar gutter is for the 4th and 5th metacarpals, and a thumb spica is for the scaphoid and thumb.

checks.q: A patient has pain in the anatomic snuffbox after falling. The wrist X-ray is read as normal. What happens next?
choices: Thumb spica splint and orthopedic follow-up
ACE wrap and discharge
No immobilization, since the film is normal
Ulnar gutter splint
checks.why: Scaphoid fractures often are not visible for 10-14 days, and a missed one can go on to avascular necrosis. A wrap or no splint leaves it unprotected, and an ulnar gutter immobilizes the wrong side of the hand.

checks.q: When splinting a boxer's fracture, why are the knuckles held bent at 70-90 degrees?
choices: To make the splint easier to wrap
Because the collateral ligaments are at their longest there, so the joints do not stiffen straight
To reduce bleeding into the hand
To keep the elbow immobilized
checks.why: Position of function keeps the MCP collateral ligaments stretched out, so the joints do not scar down in extension. It is not about wrapping ease or bleeding, and the ulnar gutter does not immobilize the elbow.

lessons.title: Lower extremity splints and cervical collars
lessons.body:
## The ankle: posterior slab plus stirrup

A **posterior short-leg splint** is a slab that runs from just below the back of the knee, down the calf, around the heel, and along the sole to the toes. The ankle is held at `90 degrees`, neutral, as if the patient were standing on a flat floor. An ankle splinted with the toes pointed down heals into a contracture that the patient then has to fight in physical therapy for weeks.

That slab alone still lets the ankle roll side to side. Add a **stirrup**, also called a sugar-tong of the leg: a strip that starts on the inner side of the calf just below the knee, passes under the heel, and comes back up the outer side. Posterior slab plus stirrup is the standard for an unstable ankle fracture. The posterior slab by itself is enough for a sprain or a small stable avulsion.

Plaster on the leg gets `12-15` layers. Mold the arch and the ankle bones with your palms, keep the toes exposed so color and sensation can be checked, and plan on a second person holding the foot at `90 degrees` while it sets, with their hand on the sole and not on the toes.

## Knee immobilizer, boot, binder

A **knee immobilizer** is a prefab foam sleeve with metal stays that holds the knee straight. Size it by length: the top sits about `10 cm` below the groin and the bottom about `10 cm` above the ankle, with straps snug enough to hold but loose enough to slide a finger under. It is used after a patellar dislocation is reduced, for some ligament injuries, and to keep a painful knee quiet in transit. It is also a trap, because a knee locked straight stiffens quickly, so patients come out of it for gentle motion as soon as the provider allows.

A **walking boot (CAM boot)** replaces a splint for stable foot and ankle injuries in a patient allowed to bear weight. It buys something a splint cannot: it comes off for skin checks and showers.

A **pelvic binder** is not a splint, but it follows the same logic. It is centered over the greater trochanters, the bony points at the top of the thighs, not up on the iliac crests, and it is tightened enough to close the pelvic ring and tamponade bleeding.

## Cervical collars in the ED

A rigid collar limits neck motion; it never eliminates it, and it only works if it is sized. Measure with your fingers laid flat from the top of the shoulder muscle (trapezius) to the bottom of the chin, then match that number of fingers to the sizing post on the collar.

Too tall pushes the head back into extension and can obstruct the neck veins. Too short lets the chin drop inside the collar, which does nothing at all. Apply it with a second person holding the head neutral, slide the back panel behind the neck first on a supine patient, seat the chin in the chin piece, then fasten.

Collars cause pressure injuries at the chin and the back of the head surprisingly fast. Any patient who is going to be in one for hours needs the skin underneath inspected, which is a two-person job with manual stabilization the whole time.

> **Key:** Ankle at `90 degrees`, toes exposed, immobilizer sized to the leg, collar sized to the neck. Every one of those is the same idea: the device only works in the right position.

> **Trap:** A pelvic binder placed up on the iliac crests does not close the pelvic ring. It belongs over the greater trochanters.

> **On shift:** Leg splints take two people. Decide who holds the foot and who wraps before anything gets dipped.
keyPoints: Posterior short-leg splint holds the ankle at 90 degrees; add a stirrup for an unstable fracture.
Lower extremity plaster is 12-15 layers; no weight bearing for 24 hours while plaster cures.
Knee immobilizer: top 10 cm below the groin, bottom 10 cm above the ankle.
Pelvic binder goes over the greater trochanters, not the iliac crests.
Collar size is measured trapezius to chin in finger widths; wrong size is worse than useless.

checks.q: Which position is correct for the ankle in a posterior short-leg splint?
choices: Toes pointed down, for comfort
Neutral at 90 degrees
Maximally dorsiflexed
Whatever position hurts least
checks.why: Neutral 90 degrees prevents an equinus contracture. Pointing the toes is comfortable but heals into a deformity, maximal dorsiflexion is not tolerated, and the least painful position is often the harmful one.

checks.q: You are asked to place a pelvic binder on a trauma patient. Where does it go?
choices: Across the umbilicus
Over the iliac crests
Centered over the greater trochanters
Around the upper thighs
checks.why: Binding at the greater trochanters closes the pelvic ring and limits bleeding. Higher placement on the crests or abdomen does not close the ring, and around the thighs does nothing to the pelvis.

lessons.title: Splint care instructions, crutches, canes and walkers
lessons.body:
## The discharge talk that prevents the return visit

Elevation is the instruction that gets skipped and matters most. Hand or foot above the level of the heart, propped on pillows, for the first `48-72 hours`. Ice over the splint `20 minutes` on and `20 minutes` off while awake for the first day or two.

Keep it dry. Wet plaster crumbles, wet padding macerates the skin underneath, and the patient cannot see what is happening in there. Two trash bags and tape will do; a proper cast cover does it better. A splint that gets soaked through needs to be changed, not dried with a hair dryer on hot.

No coat hangers, pens, chopsticks or knitting needles pushed down inside to scratch. They scrape skin nobody can see, and the wound turns up days later as an infection. Cool air from a hair dryer on the cool setting is the answer to the itch.

**Return immediately for:** numbness or pins and needles that does not resolve with elevation; fingers or toes that are pale, blue, cold, or refill slower than `2 seconds`; pain that keeps getting worse after the first day; pain out of proportion, especially when the digits are gently straightened; foul smell or drainage; or a splint that has slipped, cracked, or soaked through.

Tell them the timeline too. Most splints are a bridge to orthopedic follow-up in `3-7 days`, not the final treatment.

**The cast saw.** Patients are frightened of it and deserve a real explanation rather than a lecture. The blade does not spin. It oscillates back and forth a few millimeters, which cuts rigid plaster but skids harmlessly on soft skin. It is loud and it gets warm, and burns are possible with a dull blade or a dragging technique, which is why the operator lifts and repositions instead of plowing along.

## Fitting crutches, canes and walkers

Fit first, then teach the gait.

**Crutches.** The underarm pad sits `2 finger-widths`, about `5 cm`, below the armpit. The patient's weight rides on their hands, never on the armpit, because the nerve bundle up there (brachial plexus) gets compressed and the patient ends up with a weak, numb hand. Set the handgrips at the wrist crease with the arms hanging at the sides, which puts the elbows at `15-30 degrees` of bend. The tips rest about `15 cm` to the side and `15 cm` in front of the foot.

- **Non-weight-bearing (swing-through):** both crutches go forward, weight goes into the hands, the good leg swings past the crutches, and the injured leg never touches down.
- **Partial weight-bearing (three-point):** the crutches and the injured leg advance together, then the good leg steps through, with only the allowed amount of weight going through the injured side.
- **Stairs:** up with the good, down with the bad. Going up, the good leg leads and the crutches follow. Coming down, the crutches and the injured leg go first.

**Cane.** Held in the hand **opposite** the injured leg, so cane and bad leg swing forward together and the weight is shared across a wider base. Height at the wrist crease, elbow bent `15-30 degrees`.

**Walker.** Handgrips at the wrist crease again. The patient pushes it about a step ahead, then walks into it. They never lift and carry it, and they never haul themselves out of a chair by it, because it tips.

> **Trap:** Leaning on the axillary pads is the classic crutch mistake and it causes a real nerve injury (crutch palsy). Hands, not armpits.

> **On shift:** Watch the patient walk `10 feet` with the device before they leave. Most bad fits announce themselves in the first three steps.
keyPoints: Elevate above the heart 48-72 hours; ice 20 minutes on, 20 off; keep it dry; nothing down inside.
Return precautions: numbness, pale or cold digits, worsening pain, pain on passive stretch, drainage, wet or cracked splint.
Crutch pad 2 finger-widths (about 5 cm) below the axilla; handgrips at the wrist crease, elbows 15-30 degrees.
Stairs: up with the good leg, down with the bad leg and the crutches.
Cane goes in the hand opposite the injured leg.

checks.q: A patient rests their body weight on the tops of their crutches. What are you preventing by correcting this?
choices: Shoulder dislocation
Compression of the brachial plexus causing a weak, numb hand
Wrist fracture
Rotator cuff tear
checks.why: Axillary pressure compresses the brachial plexus and produces crutch palsy. The weight belongs on the hands. Crutch use does not cause dislocations, wrist fractures or cuff tears from this error.

checks.q: Which instruction is correct for a patient going down a flight of stairs on crutches?
choices: Good leg first, then the crutches
Crutches and injured leg first, then the good leg
Both legs together, crutches last
Hop down on the good leg without crutches
checks.why: Up with the good, down with the bad. Descending, the crutches and injured leg lead so the strong leg controls the lowering. Leading with the good leg down puts the whole body weight on a leg with nothing to catch it.

lessons.title: Wound assessment and irrigation
lessons.body:
## Describe it before you touch it

The wound description drives every decision that follows, so it comes first and it goes in the chart.

- **Size** in centimeters, measured with a ruler, not estimated.
- **Depth**, and what is visible at the bottom: fat, muscle, tendon, bone.
- **Location**, including whether it crosses a joint or a lip border.
- **Contamination**: dirt, gravel, grease, saliva, rust, glass.
- **Mechanism**: clean knife, dirty knife, crush, bite, glass, high-pressure injection. A crush or bite wound gets infected far more often than a clean cut of the same size.
- **Time since injury.** A face laceration can often be closed up to `24 hours` out because of its rich blood supply, while a contaminated wound on the lower leg may be left open at `6 hours`.
- **Distal function**: movement, sensation and pulses beyond the wound. A partly cut tendon still moves, so weakness or pain against resistance is the clue.

A patient on blood thinners, with diabetes, or with peripheral vascular disease goes in the note as well, because those change how the wound is closed and how soon it is rechecked.

## Irrigation is the whole ballgame

Infection risk is driven by how many bacteria and how much dead tissue are left behind. Antibiotics do not rescue a dirty wound. Mechanical washing does.

**Pressure.** The target is `8-15 psi`. That is what a `35-60 mL` syringe delivers when pushed firmly through an `18-19 gauge` catheter or a plastic splash guard. Pouring saline out of a bottle is roughly `0.05 psi` and accomplishes almost nothing. Pressure well above `15 psi` drives bacteria deeper and damages tissue.

**Volume.** Use about `50-100 mL per centimeter` of laceration, with the real endpoint being that the wound looks clean. A `5 cm` dirty forearm wound is a `500 mL` job, not a `100 mL` one.

**Fluid.** Warm tap water and sterile saline produce the same infection rates in simple wounds, so use what your department stocks. Warm it if you can, because cold fluid hurts and constricts vessels.

**What never goes inside a wound:** hydrogen peroxide, full-strength povidone-iodine, chlorhexidine, and alcohol. They kill the patient's own healing cells along with the bacteria. Antiseptic belongs on the intact skin **around** the wound, not in it.

**Protect yourself.** Splash guard on, face shield and gown on, absorbent pad and basin under the limb. Irrigation splash to the eyes is the most common exposure in the department and it is entirely preventable.

## Cleaning is not scrubbing

Gentle high-volume irrigation removes bacteria. Scrubbing with a brush crushes tissue and raises infection rates, so it is reserved for ground-in road rash where particles are tattooed into the skin, and then only after good anesthesia.

Hair is **clipped**, never shaved, because a razor makes micro-cuts and raises infection risk. **Eyebrows are never removed at all**, since they are the landmark for lining the wound up and they may grow back crooked or not at all.

> **Key:** Volume and pressure, not antiseptic, decide whether a wound gets infected. `8-15 psi` and roughly `100 mL` per centimeter.

> **Trap:** Hydrogen peroxide looks like it is working because it foams. The foam is tissue being destroyed. It goes nowhere near the inside of a wound.

> **On shift:** Set up the basin, pad and shield before you draw up the first syringe. Once you start, you are committed to several hundred milliliters.
keyPoints: Document size, depth, location, contamination, mechanism, time since injury and distal function.
Irrigate at 8-15 psi using a 35-60 mL syringe with an 18-19 gauge catheter or splash guard.
Volume is roughly 50-100 mL per centimeter of laceration, or until the wound looks clean.
Tap water and saline are equivalent; peroxide, alcohol and full-strength iodine never go inside a wound.
Clip hair, never shave, and never remove eyebrows.

checks.q: A 6 cm laceration from a gravel driveway needs irrigating. Which setup gives the right pressure?
choices: Pouring a liter bottle of saline over the wound
A 35-60 mL syringe with a splash guard, about 600 mL total
A 10 mL syringe with a 25 gauge needle
A pressurized water jet at 40 psi
checks.why: A 35-60 mL syringe through a splash guard delivers 8-15 psi, and 50-100 mL per cm means roughly 600 mL here. Pouring is far too low pressure, a 10 mL syringe cannot deliver the volume, and 40 psi drives bacteria deeper and injures tissue.

checks.q: Why is hydrogen peroxide not used inside a wound?
choices: It stains the tissue and hides bleeding
It is toxic to the patient's own healing cells and delays healing
It causes allergic reactions in most people
It is only effective against viruses
checks.why: Peroxide is cytotoxic to fibroblasts and healing tissue. Staining is an iodine issue, allergy is not the reason, and its antimicrobial spectrum is not the problem here.

checks.q: A patient has a scalp laceration with hair in the way. What do you do?
choices: Shave a wide margin with a razor
Clip the hair short around the wound
Shave the eyebrow line for comparison
Leave it and irrigate through the hair without clearing it
checks.why: Clipping avoids the micro-cuts a razor causes and lowers infection risk. Shaving raises infection rates, eyebrows are never removed, and hair left matted across the wound blocks both irrigation and closure.

lessons.title: The laceration tray: anesthetics, sutures, tetanus
lessons.body:
## Setting up so the provider can just sit down

On the sterile field: needle driver, toothed tissue forceps, suture scissors, gauze, a fenestrated drape, a `10 mL` syringe with a `25-27 gauge` needle for infiltration, the suture the provider asked for, and a basin. Beside the field but not on it: the anesthetic vial for someone to hold while it is drawn up, extra gauze, a light you can aim, and the irrigation setup.

## Local anesthetics, by the numbers

**Lidocaine 1%** is `10 mg per mL`. **Lidocaine 2%** is `20 mg per mL`. Onset is `2-5 minutes` and it lasts `30-120 minutes`.

Adding **epinephrine** does three useful things: the block lasts `2-3` times longer, the vessels constrict so the field is dry enough to see, and the maximum safe dose goes up.

| Drug | Maximum dose |
|---|---|
| Lidocaine, plain | `4.5 mg/kg`, about `300 mg` in an adult |
| Lidocaine with epinephrine | `7 mg/kg`, about `500 mg` |
| Bupivacaine, plain | `2.5 mg/kg` |

**Bupivacaine** starts slower, in `5-10 minutes`, but lasts `4-8 hours`, which is why it is chosen for a long repair or when the patient has to get through the night.

The old rule that epinephrine must never go near fingers, nose, ears or toes has been overturned for routine use. Commercial lidocaine with epinephrine is accepted as safe in digits for most patients. Providers still avoid it in a truly ischemic digit or severe peripheral vascular disease. Know it, but let the provider make the call.

One more thing worth knowing: a true amide anesthetic allergy is rare, and most reported "lidocaine allergies" are the racing heart and shakiness from the epinephrine.

## Suture size, material, and when it comes out

| Location | Size | Removal |
|---|---|---|
| Face | `6-0` | `3-5 days` |
| Scalp | `3-0` or `4-0` | `7-10 days` |
| Hand and fingers | `4-0` or `5-0` | `10-14 days` |
| Trunk | `3-0` or `4-0` | `7-14 days` |
| Arm or leg, over a joint | `3-0` or `4-0` | `10-14 days` |

A smaller number means thicker thread. `6-0` is hair-fine and leaves the least scar. `3-0` holds a scalp or back closed under real tension.

**Non-absorbable** suture (nylon, polypropylene) is the default for skin and must be removed. **Absorbable** suture (polyglactin, poliglecaprone, plain or chromic gut) is used in the deep layer, inside the mouth, and increasingly on children's faces so nobody has to hold a four-year-old down for removal.

**Staples** are fast and excellent for the scalp and long straight wounds on the trunk and limbs, and are not used on the face or hands. **Tissue adhesive** suits short, clean, low-tension wounds whose edges meet on their own; it is kept out of eyes, off mucosa, and off anything under tension, and it sloughs in `5-10 days`. **Adhesive strips** close tiny lacerations and support a repair after the sutures come out.

## Tetanus, on every wound

| History | Clean minor wound | All other wounds |
|---|---|---|
| 3 or more doses, last under 5 years ago | none | none |
| 3 or more doses, `5-10` years ago | none | Td or Tdap |
| 3 or more doses, over `10` years ago | Td or Tdap | Td or Tdap |
| Fewer than 3 doses, or unknown | Td or Tdap | Td or Tdap **plus** tetanus immune globulin |

Said in one line: clean wound, boost if it has been over `10` years. Dirty or deep wound, boost if it has been over `5` years. Unknown or incomplete series with a dirty wound also gets the immune globulin.

> **On the exam:** The `5`-year and `10`-year split, and immune globulin for the incompletely vaccinated patient with a dirty wound, are asked constantly.

> **Trap:** Skin glue on a wound under tension, or across a joint that bends, pops open within a day. Tension gets sutures.
keyPoints: Lidocaine 1% is 10 mg/mL; max 4.5 mg/kg plain, 7 mg/kg with epinephrine.
Bupivacaine is slower to start but lasts 4-8 hours.
Suture by site: 6-0 face, 4-0/5-0 hands, 3-0/4-0 scalp and trunk.
Removal: face 3-5 days, scalp 7-10, trunk and extremities 7-14, over joints 10-14.
Tetanus: boost at over 10 years for a clean wound, over 5 years for a dirty one; add TIG if the series is incomplete.

checks.q: A patient's last tetanus shot was 7 years ago. He has a deep puncture from a rusty nail. What does he need?
choices: Nothing
Td or Tdap only
Tetanus immune globulin only
Td or Tdap plus tetanus immune globulin
checks.why: A dirty wound is boosted at over 5 years, so he gets the vaccine. Immune globulin is added only when the primary series is incomplete or unknown, and doing nothing ignores the 5-year rule for dirty wounds.

checks.q: Which suture would you expect the provider to ask for on a 2 cm cheek laceration?
choices: 6-0 nylon
3-0 nylon
Staples
2-0 polypropylene
checks.why: Fine 6-0 suture leaves the smallest scar on the face and comes out in 3-5 days. Heavier 3-0 and 2-0 suture scars badly on the face, and staples are never used there.

checks.q: How many milligrams of lidocaine are in 10 mL of a 1% solution?
choices: 10 mg
100 mg
50 mg
checks.why: 1% means 10 mg per mL, so 10 mL contains 100 mg. 10 mg would be a single milliliter, and 1,000 mg would require 100 mL, well past the safe dose.

lessons.title: Dressings, packing, and the small procedures
lessons.body:
## Pick the dressing for the wound, not out of habit

| Dressing | Use it for |
|---|---|
| Dry gauze | A simple sutured wound with a little ooze |
| Non-adherent (Telfa, Adaptic) | Anything that would stick: abrasions, burns, skin tears |
| Petrolatum gauze | Burns and donor sites, keeping a surface moist |
| Hydrocolloid | Shallow wounds with light drainage; stays on for days |
| Hydrogel | Dry wounds that need moisture put back |
| Alginate | Heavy drainage and small oozing bleeders; it gels as it absorbs |
| Foam | Moderate to heavy drainage, and padding over bony areas |

Burns get cleaned, covered with a non-adherent or petrolatum dressing, and wrapped loosely so swelling has room. Silver sulfadiazine is still used in some departments for larger burns but is avoided on the face, in pregnancy, and with sulfa allergy, and it is not smeared on a wound a burn center will want to look at in a few hours.

Secure with tape that does not encircle a finger or limb, or with tubular net. The first dressing over a sutured wound usually comes off at `24-48 hours`.

## After an incision and drainage

An abscess is drained, not squeezed. Your part is the setup, which is an `11` blade, a hemostat for breaking up the internal pockets (loculations), a culture swab if asked, irrigation, and a great deal of gauze.

Packing, when it is used, is a wick and not a plug. A quarter-inch or half-inch plain or iodoform strip is fed in loosely with a hemostat so fluid can travel out along it, with a tail left outside and the length documented. It is removed or exchanged in `24-48 hours`, and the patient must leave knowing it is in there.

## The small procedures you will assist on

**Foreign body and splinter.** Good light, magnification, anesthesia first. Organic material like wood must come out because it causes intense inflammation and infection. X-ray finds glass and metal but usually misses wood, which shows better on ultrasound.

**Subungual hematoma.** Blood trapped under the nail after a crush, throbbing hard. Trephination, which is burning or drilling a hole through the nail with an electrocautery tip or a heated `18 gauge` needle, relieves it in seconds. There are no nerves in the nail plate, so anesthesia is often unnecessary. Stop the instant blood wells up, so the tip never reaches the nail bed.

**Nail removal** is reserved for a nail bed laceration that needs repair, or a nail already avulsed. A digital block comes first.

**Ring removal.** Try lubricant and elevation first. The **string technique** wraps suture or umbilical tape tightly around the finger from the ring outward to squeeze the swelling down, then the end is threaded under the ring and unwound, walking the ring off. If the finger is threatened or the string fails, the **ring cutter** comes out. Tell the patient the ring is being cut, document it, and hand the pieces back.

**Fishhook.** The barb is the entire problem. Common approaches are the string-yank, the advance-and-cut (push the point through the skin, cut off the barb, back it out), and the needle-cover technique. Irrigation and a tetanus check apply like any other puncture wound.

**Tick.** Fine-tipped forceps as close to the skin as possible, steady upward traction, no twisting, and none of the folklore: no petroleum jelly, no matches, no lidocaine injected around it. Clean the site and document how long it was attached and how engorged it looked, because time attached drives the Lyme decision.

> **Key:** Packing is a wick that keeps a cavity open and draining, not a cork to stop bleeding.

> **On shift:** Before trephination, warn the patient about the smell and the small pop. It is painless, but it is startling if nobody says anything.
keyPoints: Match dressing to drainage: alginate and foam for heavy, hydrogel for dry, non-adherent for anything that would stick.
Abscess packing is a loose wick with a tail left out, removed or changed in 24-48 hours.
Subungual hematoma trephination needs no anesthesia; stop as soon as blood escapes.
Ring removal: lubricant, then the string technique, then the ring cutter.
Ticks come out with fine forceps and steady upward pull, no twisting and no folk remedies.

checks.q: A patient's abscess has been drained and packed with a quarter-inch iodoform strip. What does the packing do?
choices: Stops the bleeding by plugging the cavity
Acts as a wick so the cavity keeps draining instead of sealing over
Delivers antibiotics into the bloodstream
Holds the wound edges together for healing
checks.why: Packing keeps the cavity open and wicks fluid out. It is not a hemostatic plug, it does not provide systemic antibiotics, and an abscess is deliberately left open rather than closed.

checks.q: What is the correct technique for removing an embedded tick?
choices: Cover it with petroleum jelly and wait for it to back out
Twist it counterclockwise until it releases
Grasp it at the skin with fine forceps and pull straight up with steady pressure
Touch it with a hot match head
checks.why: Steady upward traction at the skin removes the tick whole. Jelly and heat make it regurgitate and take longer, and twisting snaps off the mouthparts in the skin.

lessons.title: Urinary catheters, bladder scanning, and gastric tubes
lessons.body:
## Straight cath or indwelling

A **straight (intermittent) catheter** goes in, drains, and comes right back out. It is used for a clean urine sample, a one-time episode of retention, or a bladder that empties poorly. An **indwelling (Foley)** stays in, held by a balloon, and is used for strict output measurement in a critically ill patient, for obstruction, and for selected perioperative or comfort indications. Every additional day a Foley stays in raises infection risk, which is why somebody asks daily whether it can come out.

Size: `14` or `16 French` for a typical adult. The French number is the outside circumference in millimeters, so a bigger number is a bigger tube. A **coudé** catheter has a firm, curved tip that rides up over an enlarged prostate, which makes it the standard choice for a male patient with BPH who is hard to catheterize. The curve points toward the ceiling.

## The procedure, step by step

1. Explain it, offer a chaperone, and position and drape for dignity. Female supine with knees bent and apart; male supine with the legs straight.
2. Open the kit, set up the sterile field, and glove sterile. Your non-dominant hand becomes the dirty hand the moment it touches the patient, and it does not come back to the field.
3. Clean with the antiseptic swabs. Female: separate the labia and wipe front to back, a new swab each stroke, the opening (meatus) last. Male: retract the foreskin if present and clean in widening circles from the meatus out.
4. Lubricate generously. Where lidocaine jelly is used, it goes in a few minutes before.
5. Advance gently. Female: `5-8 cm`, or until urine returns. Male: hold the penis at about `90 degrees` to the body to straighten the urethra and advance nearly to the hub, `17-22 cm`.
6. **Wait for urine, then advance another `2-5 cm`, then inflate.** A balloon inflated in the urethra tears it.
7. Inflate with `10 mL` of **sterile water only**, from the prefilled syringe. Not saline, which can crystallize and jam the deflation channel. Not air, which floats to the top of the balloon.
8. Pull back until the balloon seats at the bladder neck, secure the tubing to the thigh with a securement device, and hang the bag **below the level of the bladder**, off the floor.

Never force against resistance. A spasm you cannot pass, blood at the meatus, a high-riding prostate, or any suspicion of urethral injury after trauma stops the attempt and gets a provider.

## The infection bundle

Insert only for a real indication. Sterile technique going in. Keep the system closed. Bag below the bladder. Secure the tube so it never tugs. Daily meatal care with soap and water. Remove it as early as possible, which is the single most effective item on the list.

## The bladder scanner

A handheld ultrasound that reads bladder volume in seconds and prevents a lot of unnecessary catheters. Supine patient, gel in the midline `2-3 cm` above the pubic bone, aim slightly toward the tailbone, take a few readings and keep the highest. Rough thresholds: a patient who cannot void with `300-400 mL` in the bladder is in retention worth draining, and a post-void residual over `300 mL` is clearly abnormal, while under `50 mL` is normal. Morbid obesity, recent abdominal surgery, ascites or a pregnant uterus make the number unreliable.

## NG and OG tubes

Measure before you open anything: the tip of the **nose** to the **earlobe** to the **xiphoid**, and mark that length on the tube. Sit the patient upright with the chin tucked, anesthetize or lubricate per protocol, and have water with a straw ready.

Advance along the floor of the nostril, straight back rather than up. At the back of the throat the patient sips and swallows, and you advance with each swallow. Stop for gagging that will not settle, coughing, a falling oxygen saturation, or a patient who suddenly cannot speak, because all of those mean the tube is heading into the airway.

Confirmation is by **X-ray**. Listening for a whoosh of air over the stomach is not confirmation, and that shortcut has killed people by allowing feeds into a lung. Nothing goes down the tube until the film has been read.

> **Key:** Urine first, then advance, then inflate, and only with sterile water. Those steps prevent the most common catheter injury there is.

> **Trap:** Auscultation confirms nothing about NG tube placement. X-ray, or the tube stays unused.
keyPoints: Adult Foley is 14-16 French; coudé tip for the male patient with BPH, curve pointed up.
Advance until urine returns, advance 2-5 cm more, then inflate with 10 mL sterile water only.
CAUTI bundle: real indication, sterile insertion, closed system, bag below the bladder, secured, removed early.
Bladder scan: 300-400 mL with inability to void means retention; post-void residual over 300 mL is abnormal.
NG length is nose to earlobe to xiphoid, and placement is confirmed by X-ray, never by auscultation.

checks.q: You are catheterizing a male patient and have advanced the catheter about 15 cm with no urine yet. What do you do?
choices: Inflate the balloon, since 15 cm is past the sphincter
Pull back and start over with a larger catheter
Continue advancing nearly to the hub and wait for urine before inflating
Inject the lidocaine jelly through the catheter
checks.why: The male urethra is 17-22 cm, so 15 cm can still be short of the bladder. The balloon is inflated only after urine returns; inflating early tears the urethra. Restarting with a bigger catheter does not solve a length problem.

checks.q: What fluid is used to inflate a Foley balloon?
choices: Sterile water
Normal saline
Air
Sterile water mixed with antibiotic
checks.why: Sterile water is the standard. Saline can crystallize and block the deflation channel, air floats and leaves the balloon seated unevenly, and nothing is added to the balloon fluid.

checks.q: An NG tube is at the marked depth and the nurse asks you to push a feed. The X-ray has not been read. What is correct?
choices: Push air and listen over the stomach to confirm, then feed
Aspirate and check the color, then feed
Nothing goes down the tube until the X-ray is read
Feed slowly and watch for coughing
checks.why: Radiographic confirmation is the standard before use. Auscultation is unreliable and has caused deaths from feeding into a lung, aspirate appearance is not confirmatory, and feeding slowly does not make a misplaced tube safe.

lessons.title: Irrigations, reductions, sedation setup, and sterile technique
lessons.body:
## Eye irrigation starts at the door

A chemical in the eye is one of the few true treat-before-you-register emergencies. Irrigation starts immediately, before visual acuity, before registration.

**Alkali is worse than acid.** Acids burn the surface and the damaged protein forms something of a barrier. Alkalis (drain cleaner, lye, oven cleaner, wet cement, ammonia) dissolve cell membranes and keep tunneling deeper for as long as they are present.

Order of work: topical anesthetic drops first, because nobody can hold an acid-burned eye open. Check the pH with a strip in the lower lid pocket. Then set up the **Morgan lens**, a contact-lens-shaped irrigator that sits on the eye and spreads fluid across the whole surface. Run it off normal saline or lactated Ringer's through IV tubing, start the flow **before** it goes in and stop the flow **before** it comes out, and seat it under the upper lid first, then down under the lower lid.

Run at least `1-2 liters` for a chemical exposure, often much more. Sweep the lid pockets for particles, because cement and lime leave grit that keeps burning. Then stop, wait `5-10 minutes` for the surface to equilibrate, and recheck the pH. **The goal is `7.0-7.4`.** Checking the second you stop measures the irrigation fluid, not the eye.

## Ear irrigation for wax

Body-temperature water, or water mixed with hydrogen peroxide, delivered through a syringe and soft catheter aimed at the canal wall rather than the eardrum, with a basin under the ear. Temperature matters: fluid that is cold or hot on the drum sets off vertigo and vomiting.

**Do not irrigate** with any chance of a perforated drum, with tympanostomy tubes, after ear surgery, with an object that swells in water such as a bean or paper, with a button battery, or with an already inflamed canal. Those get a provider and direct visualization.

## Reductions and procedural sedation

For a shoulder, patella or nursemaid's elbow reduction, your job is the room: imaging up on the screen, bed at the right height, sheets for counter-traction if asked, the monitor on, and post-reduction imaging plus a repeat neurovascular check ready to go. A **nursemaid's elbow** in a toddler usually takes nothing but the provider's hands and no sedation at all. A dislocated patella often reduces as the knee is straightened.

If sedation is planned, the room is set before a single milligram is pushed:

- Suction on, tested, Yankauer within reach
- Bag-valve-mask and oxygen at the head of the bed, airway adjuncts out of the wrapper
- Monitor on: continuous pulse oximetry, cardiac monitor, blood pressure cycling, and **end-tidal CO2**, which shows apnea long before the oximeter does
- Defibrillator pads or the defibrillator at the bedside per policy
- Reversal agents available: naloxone for opioids, flumazenil for benzodiazepines
- IV patent and running
- Everyone stops for the **time-out**: right patient, right procedure, right site, consent, allergies, and who is watching the airway

## Positioning is a skill of its own

| Procedure | Position |
|---|---|
| Lumbar puncture | Lateral decubitus, knees to chest, chin down, hips and shoulders stacked square; or sitting and leaning over a table |
| Pelvic exam | Lithotomy, drape over the knees, chaperone present |
| Rectal exam | Left lateral with the upper knee drawn up |
| Central line, subclavian or internal jugular | Supine, head down about `15 degrees` (Trendelenburg), head turned away |
| Chest tube | Supine, arm raised above the head, bed tilted slightly head-up |

For the lumbar puncture the success of the tap is largely in your hands. The spine has to be curled like a shrimp with the hips square, and you hold the patient there while they are uncomfortable. Coach the breathing, keep your hands off the sterile field, and warn before any movement.

## Sterile field rules for everyone at the bedside

- Only the top surface of a draped field is sterile, and a `2.5 cm` border around the edge is not.
- Never turn your back on the field.
- Never reach across it. Walk around.
- Wet is contaminated, because fluid wicks bacteria straight through a drape.
- Keep your hands above waist level and in front of you.
- Anything you are unsure about is contaminated. Say so out loud and replace it.

> **Key:** Saying "I think I broke sterility" costs thirty seconds. Not saying it costs the patient an infection.

> **On shift:** Offer a chaperone for every sensitive exam, document who it was, and expose only the part being examined. That protects the patient and the provider at the same time.
keyPoints: Chemical eye exposure: anesthetic drops, Morgan lens, at least 1-2 L, recheck pH 5-10 minutes after stopping, goal 7.0-7.4.
Alkali burns are worse than acid because they keep penetrating.
Do not irrigate an ear with a possible perforation, tubes, a button battery or a swelling object.
Sedation setup: suction, BVM and oxygen, monitor with EtCO2, pads, reversal agents, IV, and the time-out.
Sterile field: 2.5 cm border is not sterile, never turn your back or reach across, wet means contaminated.

checks.q: After irrigating a lye splash with 2 liters, when do you recheck the eye pH?
choices: Immediately as the fluid stops
5-10 minutes after stopping the irrigation
One hour later
Only if the patient still has pain
checks.why: Waiting 5-10 minutes lets the surface equilibrate, so the strip reads the eye rather than the leftover irrigation fluid. Checking immediately gives a falsely normal number, an hour is far too long, and pain is an unreliable endpoint after anesthetic drops.

checks.q: Which item on the procedural sedation setup detects apnea earliest?
choices: Pulse oximeter
Blood pressure cuff cycling every 3 minutes
End-tidal CO2 monitoring
Cardiac monitor
checks.why: EtCO2 shows a lost waveform the moment breathing stops, while oxygen saturation lags by a minute or more, especially on supplemental oxygen. Blood pressure and rhythm change even later.

checks.q: You are holding a patient for a lumbar puncture and your sleeve brushes the edge of the sterile drape. What do you do?
choices: Say nothing; the outer edge does not count
Announce it so the field can be corrected
Wipe the spot with alcohol
Move your arm back and continue
checks.why: A contamination that is announced costs seconds to fix. The edge border is specifically not sterile, wiping with alcohol does not restore sterility, and quietly continuing risks meningitis in a patient having a needle placed near the spinal canal.

cards.front: Which joints must a splint cross?
cards.back: The joint above and the joint below the injury. Anything less lets the fracture keep moving.

cards.front: What are the three parts of a neurovascular check?
cards.back: Circulation (pulse, color, warmth, cap refill under 2 seconds), motor (movement of the digits), and sensation (light touch on both sides of each digit).

cards.front: When is the neurovascular check documented on a splinted limb?
cards.back: Before the splint goes on and again after it is wrapped, both with a time.

cards.front: What is the position of function for the hand?
cards.back: Wrist extended 20-30 degrees, MCP knuckles bent 70-90 degrees, finger joints nearly straight, thumb abducted as if holding a soda can.

cards.front: Why is rigid material never wrapped fully around a fresh injury?
cards.back: A circumferential cast on a swelling limb can cause compartment syndrome. A splint stays rigid on one or two sides with elastic wrap around the rest.

cards.front: What is the earliest reliable sign of compartment syndrome?
cards.back: Pain out of proportion to the injury, especially pain on passive stretch of the fingers or toes. A lost pulse is a very late sign.

cards.front: How many plaster layers for an upper versus lower extremity splint?
cards.back: Upper extremity 8-10 layers, lower extremity 12-15 layers.

cards.front: What dip water temperature is used for plaster, and why does it matter?
cards.back: Warm, roughly 20-25 degrees C. Plaster cures exothermically, so hot water plus thick layers plus insulation can cause real burns.

cards.front: Why is a curing splint never laid on a pillow?
cards.back: The padding traps the heat of the exothermic reaction against the skin and can burn the patient.

cards.front: How long does plaster take to reach full strength?
cards.back: Workable 2-4 minutes, firm at 10-15 minutes, full strength at 24 hours. No weight bearing on a leg splint for a day.

cards.front: How fast does fiberglass set compared with plaster?
cards.back: Rigid in 3-5 minutes and near full strength in about 30 minutes, much faster than plaster.

cards.front: In what direction is an elastic bandage wrapped over a splint?
cards.back: Distal to proximal, half-overlapping each turn, snug without full-tension stretch, so swelling is pushed toward the heart.

cards.front: Which limb do you measure the splint material against?
cards.back: The uninjured limb. Measuring on the injured side means moving the fracture.

cards.front: Why mold a setting splint with palms rather than fingertips?
cards.back: Fingertips leave divots in the material, and those divots become pressure points and pressure sores.

cards.front: How much padding goes under a splint?
cards.back: Stockinette, then 2-3 layers of Webril rolled distal to proximal with half-overlap, extra over bony points and 2 extra turns at each end.

cards.front: Which splint is used for a distal radius fracture, and why that one?
cards.back: Sugar-tong. It crosses the elbow, which is the only way to block forearm rotation (supination and pronation).

cards.front: A patient has snuffbox tenderness but a normal wrist X-ray. What splint?
cards.back: Thumb spica with orthopedic follow-up. Scaphoid fractures often are invisible for 10-14 days and a missed one can go on to avascular necrosis.

cards.front: Which splint goes on a boxer's fracture?
cards.back: Ulnar gutter, covering the ring and little fingers, with the MCPs bent 70-90 degrees and padding between the fingers.

cards.front: Which splint is used for a 2nd or 3rd metacarpal fracture?
cards.back: Radial gutter, covering the index and middle fingers, with a hole cut for the thumb.

cards.front: Which splint is used for a humeral shaft fracture?
cards.back: Coaptation splint, a U from the shoulder around the elbow, always combined with a sling and swathe.

cards.front: What is the difference between a sling and a swathe?
cards.back: The sling carries the weight of the forearm; the swathe is the strap around the chest that stops the arm swinging. Shoulder and humerus injuries need both.

cards.front: What is buddy taping and when is it appropriate?
cards.back: Taping an injured finger to its neighbor with gauze between them. Used for stable sprains and non-displaced phalanx fractures, and it lets the finger keep moving.

cards.front: At what angle is the ankle held in a posterior short-leg splint?
cards.back: Neutral, 90 degrees, as if standing on a flat floor. Splinting with the toes pointed down causes a contracture.

cards.front: What does a stirrup add to a posterior short-leg splint?
cards.back: It blocks side-to-side rolling of the ankle. Posterior slab plus stirrup is standard for an unstable ankle fracture.

cards.front: How is a knee immobilizer sized?
cards.back: Top about 10 cm below the groin, bottom about 10 cm above the ankle, straps snug with room to slide a finger underneath.

cards.front: Where is a pelvic binder positioned?
cards.back: Centered over the greater trochanters, not the iliac crests, tight enough to close the pelvic ring.

cards.front: How is a rigid cervical collar sized?
cards.back: Fingers laid flat measure from the top of the trapezius to the bottom of the chin, then that number is matched to the collar's sizing post.

cards.front: What goes wrong with a collar that is too tall or too short?
cards.back: Too tall extends the neck and can obstruct venous drainage; too short lets the chin slip inside so the collar does nothing.

cards.front: How high should the underarm pad of a crutch sit?
cards.back: Two finger-widths, about 5 cm, below the armpit, with the patient's weight carried on the hands.

cards.front: Where are crutch and cane handgrips set?
cards.back: At the wrist crease with the arms hanging at the sides, which puts the elbows at 15-30 degrees of flexion.

cards.front: What injury does leaning on the axillary crutch pads cause?
cards.back: Crutch palsy: compression of the brachial plexus producing a weak, numb hand.

cards.front: What is the rule for crutches on stairs?
cards.back: Up with the good, down with the bad. Going up, the good leg leads; coming down, the crutches and injured leg go first.

cards.front: Which hand holds a cane?
cards.back: The hand opposite the injured leg, so the cane and the bad leg advance together and the weight spreads over a wider base.

cards.front: How long should a patient elevate a new splint?
cards.back: Above the level of the heart for the first 48-72 hours, with ice 20 minutes on and 20 minutes off while awake for the first day or two.

cards.front: Why does a cast saw not cut skin?
cards.back: The blade oscillates back and forth a few millimeters rather than spinning, so it cuts rigid plaster but skids on soft skin. It can still burn if dull or dragged.

cards.front: Name three splint return precautions a patient must be given.
cards.back: Numbness that will not clear with elevation, digits that are pale, blue or cold, and pain that keeps worsening or hurts on passive stretch. Also drainage, smell, or a wet or cracked splint.

cards.front: What irrigation pressure cleans a wound, and how do you produce it?
cards.back: 8-15 psi, made with a 35-60 mL syringe pushed through an 18-19 gauge catheter or a splash guard.

cards.front: How much irrigation fluid does a laceration need?
cards.back: About 50-100 mL per centimeter of laceration, with the real endpoint being a wound that looks clean.

cards.front: Tap water or sterile saline for wound irrigation?
cards.back: Either. Infection rates are the same in simple wounds, so use what the department stocks, warmed if possible.

cards.front: What must never be put inside a wound?
cards.back: Hydrogen peroxide, full-strength povidone-iodine, chlorhexidine and alcohol. They kill healing cells. Antiseptic goes on the intact skin around the wound.

cards.front: Clip or shave hair around a wound?
cards.back: Clip. A razor makes micro-cuts and raises infection risk. Eyebrows are never removed at all, because they are the alignment landmark.

cards.front: What must be documented about a wound before it is cleaned?
cards.back: Size in centimeters, depth and what is visible at the base, location, contamination, mechanism, time since injury, and distal movement, sensation and pulses.

cards.front: How many mg of lidocaine are in 1 mL of 1% and of 2%?
cards.back: 1% is 10 mg per mL and 2% is 20 mg per mL.

cards.front: What are the maximum doses of lidocaine with and without epinephrine?
cards.back: 4.5 mg/kg plain, about 300 mg in an adult, and 7 mg/kg with epinephrine, about 500 mg.

cards.front: What does adding epinephrine to a local anesthetic accomplish?
cards.back: It makes the block last 2-3 times longer, constricts vessels so the field is dry, and raises the maximum safe dose.

cards.front: Is lidocaine with epinephrine acceptable in fingers, ears and the nose?
cards.back: Yes for most patients; the old prohibition has been overturned. It is still avoided in a truly ischemic digit or severe peripheral vascular disease. The provider decides.

cards.front: When would a provider choose bupivacaine over lidocaine?
cards.back: For a long repair or overnight relief. It starts in 5-10 minutes but lasts 4-8 hours. Max dose 2.5 mg/kg plain.

cards.front: What suture sizes go on the face, hands, scalp and trunk?
cards.back: Face 6-0; hands 4-0 or 5-0; scalp and trunk 3-0 or 4-0. A smaller number means thicker thread.

cards.front: When do sutures come out by site?
cards.back: Face 3-5 days, scalp 7-10 days, trunk and extremities 7-14 days, hands and anything over a joint 10-14 days.

cards.front: Where are staples appropriate and where are they not?
cards.back: Good for the scalp and long straight wounds on the trunk and limbs. Never on the face or hands.

cards.front: Which wounds suit tissue adhesive?
cards.back: Short, clean, low-tension wounds whose edges meet on their own. Keep it out of eyes and off mucosa; it sloughs in 5-10 days. Not for wounds under tension or over bending joints.

cards.front: State the tetanus booster rule in one line.
cards.back: Clean minor wound: boost if the last dose was over 10 years ago. Dirty or deep wound: boost if over 5 years ago.

cards.front: Who gets tetanus immune globulin?
cards.back: A patient with a dirty or deep wound whose primary series is fewer than three doses or unknown. They get the vaccine as well.

cards.front: Which dressing for a heavily draining wound, and which for a dry one?
cards.back: Alginate or foam for heavy drainage; hydrogel to put moisture back into a dry wound.

cards.front: What is the purpose of packing after an incision and drainage?
cards.back: It is a wick that keeps the cavity open and draining, not a plug. It is placed loosely, a tail is left out, the length is documented, and it is changed in 24-48 hours.

cards.front: How is a subungual hematoma relieved?
cards.back: Trephination, burning or drilling a hole through the nail plate with electrocautery or a heated 18 gauge needle. No anesthesia needed; stop as soon as blood escapes.

cards.front: Which imaging finds a retained wooden foreign body?
cards.back: Ultrasound. Plain X-ray shows glass and metal but usually misses wood.

cards.front: Describe the string technique for ring removal.
cards.back: Wrap suture or umbilical tape tightly around the finger from the ring outward to compress the swelling, thread the end under the ring, then unwind it to walk the ring off.

cards.front: How is an attached tick removed?
cards.back: Fine-tipped forceps at the skin, steady upward traction, no twisting. No petroleum jelly, matches or injected lidocaine. Document how long it was attached.

cards.front: What size Foley for a typical adult, and what is a coudé for?
cards.back: 14 or 16 French. A coudé has a firm curved tip that rides over an enlarged prostate, used for the male patient with BPH, curve pointed up.

cards.front: When is a Foley balloon inflated, and with what?
cards.back: Only after urine returns and the catheter is advanced another 2-5 cm. Inflate with 10 mL of sterile water, never saline and never air.

cards.front: How far is a catheter advanced in a male versus a female patient?
cards.back: Male: nearly to the hub, 17-22 cm, with the penis held at about 90 degrees. Female: 5-8 cm or until urine returns.

cards.front: List the CAUTI prevention bundle.
cards.back: Insert only for a real indication, sterile insertion, closed system, bag below the bladder and off the floor, tubing secured, daily meatal care, and remove as early as possible.

cards.front: What bladder scan volumes suggest urinary retention?
cards.back: 300-400 mL with an inability to void is retention worth draining. A post-void residual over 300 mL is clearly abnormal; under 50 mL is normal.

cards.front: How is NG tube insertion length measured?
cards.back: Tip of the nose to the earlobe to the xiphoid process, marked on the tube before insertion.

cards.front: How is NG tube placement confirmed?
cards.back: By X-ray. Auscultating a whoosh of air over the stomach is not confirmation, and nothing goes down the tube until the film is read.

cards.front: What is the target pH after irrigating a chemical eye exposure?
cards.back: 7.0-7.4, checked 5-10 minutes after the irrigation is stopped so the strip reads the eye rather than the fluid.

cards.front: Why is an alkali eye burn worse than an acid burn?
cards.back: Alkalis dissolve cell membranes and keep penetrating deeper, while acids coagulate surface protein that partly limits the injury.

cards.front: What goes in the eye before a Morgan lens?
cards.back: Topical anesthetic drops, because the eye cannot be held open otherwise. Start the flow before inserting and stop the flow before removing.

cards.front: When should an ear NOT be irrigated?
cards.back: Possible perforated drum, tympanostomy tubes, previous ear surgery, an object that swells in water, a button battery, or an already inflamed canal.

cards.front: What monitoring detects apnea first during procedural sedation?
cards.back: End-tidal CO2. The waveform disappears immediately, while pulse oximetry lags by a minute or more, especially on supplemental oxygen.

cards.front: What must be at the bedside before procedural sedation begins?
cards.back: Working suction, BVM and oxygen, airway adjuncts, monitor with EtCO2, defibrillator or pads per policy, reversal agents, a patent IV, and a completed time-out.

cards.front: How do you position a patient for a lumbar puncture?
cards.back: Lateral decubitus curled like a shrimp, knees to chest and chin down with hips and shoulders stacked square, or sitting and leaning forward over a table.

cards.front: What position is used for central line placement in the neck or chest?
cards.back: Supine with the head down about 15 degrees (Trendelenburg) and the head turned away, which fills the vein and reduces air embolism risk.

cards.front: Name four sterile field rules for anyone at the bedside.
cards.back: Only the top of the drape is sterile and a 2.5 cm border is not; never turn your back on the field; never reach across it; wet means contaminated.

quiz.q: A 28-year-old has a mid-shaft forearm fracture. Which principle determines how far the splint must extend?
choices: It must cover only the fracture site
It must immobilize the joint above and the joint below
It must extend to the shoulder
It must stop at the wrist crease
quiz.why: Immobilizing the joint above and below is what actually stops motion at the fracture. Covering only the fracture lets both joints move it, extending to the shoulder is unnecessary for a forearm, and stopping at the wrist leaves the fracture free.

quiz.q: Twenty minutes after you apply a forearm splint, the patient reports severe pain that is worse when you gently straighten his fingers. What is the concern?
choices: Normal post-injury pain
A poorly molded splint
Compartment syndrome
Nerve laceration from the original injury
quiz.why: Pain out of proportion, especially on passive stretch, is the earliest sign of compartment syndrome and demands immediate action. Normal pain eases with elevation, molding problems cause focal pressure pain, and a nerve laceration causes numbness rather than escalating stretch pain.

quiz.q: Which of the following counts as a complete neurovascular check of a splinted hand?
choices: Radial pulse, finger movement, and light touch sensation on each finger
Radial pulse alone
Capillary refill and skin color only
Asking whether the splint feels tight
quiz.why: Circulation, motor and sensation are three separate findings and all three are documented. A pulse alone misses nerve injury, refill and color cover only circulation, and a subjective tightness question tests nothing.

quiz.q: A tech applies 24 layers of plaster dipped in hot water to a forearm and rests the curing splint on a pillow. What is the most likely complication?
choices: The splint will not harden
The plaster will crack as it dries
The splint will be too light to immobilize
A thermal burn to the skin under the splint
quiz.why: Excess layers, hot water and insulation all add to the exothermic heat and cause real burns. Hot water speeds rather than prevents hardening, cracking is not the issue with thick plaster, and 24 layers is anything but too light.

quiz.q: How many layers of plaster are typically used for a lower extremity splint?
choices: 30 or more
quiz.why: Lower extremity splints use 12-15 layers against 8-10 for the upper extremity. Four to six is too weak to hold a leg, and anything over about 20 layers raises the burn risk without adding useful strength.

quiz.q: You finish a splint and the patient's fingers become dusky and cool within minutes. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The plaster is still curing
The patient is anxious
The elastic wrap was applied too tightly or proximal to distal
The stockinette was too long
quiz.why: A wrap that is too tight or applied toward the hand obstructs venous return and produces dusky, cool fingers. Curing plaster produces warmth, not duskiness; anxiety does not change perfusion this way; and extra stockinette is padded out of the way.

quiz.q: A 45-year-old fell on an outstretched hand. X-ray shows a non-displaced distal radius fracture. Which splint does this need?
choices: Sugar-tong forearm splint
Volar forearm splint
Ulnar gutter splint
Posterior long-arm splint
quiz.why: Sugar-tong crosses the elbow and blocks rotation, which is exactly what a distal radius fracture needs. A volar splint does not cross the elbow, an ulnar gutter is for the 4th and 5th metacarpals, and a long-arm splint is for elbow and proximal forearm injuries.

quiz.q: Which injury is splinted with a thumb spica?
choices: Fifth metacarpal neck fracture
Olecranon fracture
Distal phalanx crush of the index finger
Suspected scaphoid fracture
quiz.why: A thumb spica immobilizes the wrist and thumb for scaphoid injuries and thumb ulnar collateral ligament tears. A fifth metacarpal fracture gets an ulnar gutter, an olecranon fracture gets a long-arm splint, and a fingertip crush gets a finger splint.

quiz.q: A 19-year-old punched a wall and has a fractured fifth metacarpal neck. Which position must the splint hold?
choices: Fingers fully extended for comfort
Wrist flexed 30 degrees with fingers straight
Wrist extended about 20 degrees with the MCP joints bent 70-90 degrees
Wrist neutral with the fingers curled into a fist
quiz.why: Position of function keeps the MCP collateral ligaments at length so the knuckles do not stiffen straight. Full extension is the classic error, wrist flexion increases pressure in the carpal tunnel, and a closed fist cannot be maintained or inspected.

quiz.q: A patient with a humeral shaft fracture is placed in a coaptation splint. What else does the provider expect?
choices: A cervical collar
A sling and swathe
A knee immobilizer
A figure-of-eight clavicle strap
quiz.why: Coaptation splints are paired with a sling to carry the forearm's weight and a swathe to stop the arm swinging. A collar is for the neck, a knee immobilizer for the leg, and a figure-of-eight strap is for clavicle fractures.

quiz.q: While you build a posterior short-leg splint, the assistant lets the foot drop so the toes point downward as the plaster sets. What is the consequence?
choices: The splint will be stronger
Nothing, the position self-corrects
The ankle swells less
The ankle heals in equinus and needs therapy to recover motion
quiz.why: Setting the ankle in plantar flexion produces an equinus contracture the patient must work out of in physical therapy. Position does not change splint strength or swelling, and hardened plaster does not self-correct.

quiz.q: A trauma patient has an unstable pelvis. Where do you place the binder?
choices: Centered over the greater trochanters
Over the iliac crests
At the level of the umbilicus
Around the proximal thighs
quiz.why: The greater trochanters are the level at which a binder closes the pelvic ring and limits bleeding. Higher placement at the crests or umbilicus does not close the ring, and the thighs are below the pelvis entirely.

quiz.q: A cervical collar is applied that is one size too tall. What happens?
choices: The patient is more comfortable
It works the same as a correctly sized collar
It extends the neck and can obstruct venous drainage
It allows the chin to slip inside the collar
quiz.why: An oversized collar hyperextends the neck and can compress the jugular veins. Comfort is not the point, an incorrectly sized collar does not immobilize properly, and chin slippage is the problem with a collar that is too short.

quiz.q: You are fitting crutches for a patient with a non-weight-bearing ankle fracture. Where do the underarm pads sit?
choices: Firmly against the armpit
About two finger-widths below the armpit
At the level of the nipple line
Wherever the patient says is comfortable
quiz.why: Two finger-widths, roughly 5 cm, keeps weight off the brachial plexus and prevents crutch palsy. Pads pressed into the axilla cause the nerve injury, the nipple line is far too low, and comfort alone often produces the harmful setting.

quiz.q: Which instruction is correct for a patient using a cane after a left knee injury?
choices: Hold the cane in the right hand
Hold the cane in the left hand
Alternate hands every few steps
Use two canes regardless
quiz.why: The cane goes in the hand opposite the injured leg so the two advance together and the load is shared. Holding it on the injured side narrows the base and does not unload the knee, alternating destabilizes gait, and two canes are not the default.

quiz.q: A patient with a new leg splint asks when he can walk on it. What do you tell him?
choices: Immediately, as soon as it feels firm
After 10-15 minutes when it is firm to touch
Any time, since fiberglass is instantly strong
Not for 24 hours, until the plaster reaches full strength
quiz.why: Plaster is firm in 10-15 minutes but does not reach full strength for 24 hours, so weight bearing is deferred. Firm to touch is not fully cured, and fiberglass, while faster, still takes about 30 minutes and is not what was applied here.

quiz.q: An 8 cm laceration from a fall in a parking lot is being prepared for repair. How much irrigation is appropriate?
choices: About 100 mL
About 800 mL
About 50 mL
None, since the wound will be sutured
quiz.why: At 50-100 mL per centimeter, an 8 cm contaminated wound needs roughly 400-800 mL. One hundred or fifty milliliters is far too little for a contaminated wound this long, and skipping irrigation before closure buries bacteria under the sutures.

quiz.q: Which setup delivers wound irrigation in the 8-15 psi range?
choices: A 1 L saline bottle poured over the wound
A bulb syringe
A 35-60 mL syringe with a splash guard or 18-19 gauge catheter
A high-pressure surgical lavage at 50 psi
quiz.why: That syringe and orifice combination produces 8-15 psi. Pouring and bulb syringes deliver almost no pressure, and 50 psi damages tissue and drives bacteria deeper into the wound.

quiz.q: A nurse asks you to pour hydrogen peroxide into a fresh laceration. What is the correct response?
choices: Do it, since the foaming shows it is working
Dilute it by half first
Use it only on the deepest part
Do not put it in the wound, because it is toxic to healing tissue
quiz.why: Peroxide is cytotoxic to fibroblasts and delays healing; the foam is tissue reacting, not evidence of benefit. Dilution and partial application do not change the mechanism of harm. Antiseptic belongs on intact skin around the wound.

quiz.q: A patient with a scalp laceration has hair obscuring the wound. What is correct?
choices: Clip the hair short around the wound
Shave the area with a disposable razor
