Shave a wide margin including the eyebrow for symmetry
Irrigate through the hair without moving it
quiz.why: Clipping avoids the micro-cuts that raise infection risk after shaving. Eyebrows are never removed because they guide alignment and may not grow back, and hair left across the wound blocks both cleaning and closure.

quiz.q: A 60 kg adult is getting a large laceration repaired. What is the maximum dose of plain lidocaine?
choices: About 120 mg
About 200 mg
About 270 mg
About 420 mg
quiz.why: Plain lidocaine is 4.5 mg/kg, so 60 kg allows about 270 mg, and the adult ceiling is 300 mg no matter the weight. About 420 mg corresponds to the 7 mg/kg limit that applies only when epinephrine is added, and the lower figures underdose the repair unnecessarily.

quiz.q: A provider asks for an anesthetic that will keep a painful hand repair comfortable overnight. Which is most appropriate?
choices: Lidocaine 1% plain
Bupivacaine
Lidocaine 2% plain
Topical anesthetic gel alone
quiz.why: Bupivacaine lasts 4-8 hours, far longer than lidocaine's 30-120 minutes at either concentration. Topical gel alone will not anesthetize a deep repair.

quiz.q: A 3 cm laceration on the cheek is being repaired. Which suture and removal timing should you anticipate?
choices: 6-0 nylon, out in 3-5 days
3-0 nylon, out in 14 days
Staples, out in 10 days
4-0 nylon, out in 14 days
quiz.why: Facial wounds get fine 6-0 suture removed at 3-5 days to minimize scarring and suture marks. Heavier suture and prolonged removal scar the face, and staples are never used there.

quiz.q: A patient with a deep, soil-contaminated puncture says he has never had a tetanus shot. What does he need?
choices: No treatment, since the wound is small
Td or Tdap only
Tetanus immune globulin only
Td or Tdap plus tetanus immune globulin
quiz.why: A dirty wound with fewer than three prior doses gets both the vaccine to start immunity and immune globulin for immediate protection. Either one alone leaves a gap, and depth and contamination make this anything but a minor wound.

quiz.q: A patient's last tetanus booster was 8 years ago and she has a clean 2 cm kitchen knife cut. What is required?
choices: Td or Tdap now
No tetanus intervention
Tetanus immune globulin
Both vaccine and immune globulin
quiz.why: A clean minor wound in a fully vaccinated patient needs a booster only after 10 years, so 8 years requires nothing. The 5-year rule applies to dirty wounds, and immune globulin is only for incomplete or unknown vaccination with a dirty wound.

quiz.q: An abscess has been incised and drained and the provider asks for packing. What is the purpose of the packing strip?
choices: To stop bleeding by filling the cavity
To deliver antibiotics locally into the bloodstream
To wick fluid out and keep the cavity from sealing over
To approximate the wound edges for primary closure
quiz.why: Packing keeps the cavity open and draining until the base heals upward. It is not a hemostatic plug, it provides no systemic antibiotic, and an abscess is deliberately left open rather than closed.

quiz.q: A carpenter has a splinter of wood embedded in his palm and the X-ray is negative. What does that mean?
choices: There is no foreign body
The splinter has already dissolved
A negative X-ray rules out infection risk
Wood is often invisible on X-ray, so imaging does not exclude it
quiz.why: Plain films show glass and metal but frequently miss wood, which is better seen on ultrasound. A negative film does not exclude a retained organic foreign body, which causes intense inflammation and infection if left.

quiz.q: A patient has a painful subungual hematoma after slamming a finger in a door. What relieves it?
choices: Trephination of the nail plate with cautery or a heated needle
Immediate nail removal under a digital block
A compression wrap around the fingertip
Splinting the finger for two weeks
quiz.why: Burning or drilling a hole through the nail releases the pressure within seconds and usually needs no anesthesia. Nail removal is reserved for a nail bed laceration needing repair, and compression or splinting does nothing for trapped blood.

quiz.q: A patient has a swollen finger with a wedding ring cutting in, and lubricant has failed. What is the next reasonable step?
choices: Cut the ring immediately without discussion
Wait and reassess in two hours
Try the string technique to compress the swelling and walk the ring off
Apply ice for 30 minutes and send the patient home
quiz.why: The string technique squeezes the edema down and slides the ring off without destroying it. Cutting is the fallback, not the first move, and delaying or discharging a finger that is being constricted risks ischemia.

quiz.q: You are catheterizing a female patient. Urine returns when the catheter is 6 cm in. What comes next?
choices: Inflate the balloon right away at 6 cm
Advance another 2-5 cm, then inflate with 10 mL of sterile water
Withdraw 2 cm, then inflate
Inflate with 10 mL of normal saline
quiz.why: Advancing a little further guarantees the balloon is in the bladder and not the urethra, and it is filled with sterile water. Inflating at the moment urine appears risks urethral injury, withdrawing moves it back out, and saline can crystallize and lock the balloon.

quiz.q: A 74-year-old man with known BPH cannot be catheterized with a standard 16 French Foley. What does the provider likely ask for?
choices: A coudé catheter with the tip curved upward
A 22 French straight catheter forced past the resistance
A pediatric 8 French catheter
Repeat attempts with more lubricant and firm pressure
quiz.why: The firm, curved coudé tip rides over an enlarged prostate. Forcing any catheter risks creating a false passage, a pediatric catheter is too soft to negotiate the prostate, and repeated forceful attempts cause urethral trauma and bleeding.

quiz.q: A patient says she cannot urinate. The bladder scanner reads 380 mL. What does this suggest?
choices: A normal bladder volume needing no action
Dehydration
Scanner error requiring no follow-up
Urinary retention that likely needs draining
quiz.why: 300-400 mL in a patient who cannot void is retention worth draining. A normal post-void residual is under 50 mL, dehydration would produce a low volume, and dismissing the reading leaves a distended bladder untreated.

quiz.q: A worker splashed wet cement in his eye. Which sequence is correct?
choices: Check visual acuity, register the patient, then irrigate
Topical anesthetic, check pH, begin Morgan lens irrigation with at least 1-2 L
Irrigate with 250 mL and recheck pH immediately
Patch the eye and wait for the provider
quiz.why: Alkali exposure is irrigated immediately after anesthetic drops, with pH guiding the endpoint and 1-2 L as a minimum. Delaying for acuity or registration lets the alkali keep penetrating, 250 mL is far too little, and patching traps the chemical against the eye.

quiz.q: During procedural sedation for a shoulder reduction, which monitor alerts you to apnea soonest?
choices: The blood pressure cuff
The cardiac monitor
End-tidal CO2 waveform
The pulse oximeter
quiz.why: The capnography waveform disappears the moment ventilation stops, while oxygen saturation lags by a minute or more on supplemental oxygen. Blood pressure and rhythm change later still, after hypoxia is already established.

scenarios.title: Room 9: 52-year-old, fall on ice, deformed wrist
scenarios.intro: A 52-year-old woman slipped on an icy step an hour ago and landed on her outstretched right hand. She is holding her forearm across her body. The wrist has an obvious dinner-fork deformity. The provider has already seen her, X-ray shows a non-displaced distal radius fracture, and the order reads: **splint and discharge with orthopedic follow-up**. You are the tech assigned to the room.

steps.prompt: You walk in with the splint cart. She is holding the arm still and asks how long this will take. What is the first thing you do?

choices.text: Check and document circulation, motor and sensation in the right hand, with a time
choices.feedback: Correct. The pre-splint neurovascular check is your baseline. Without it, you cannot prove whether anything you do makes the hand worse.

choices.text: Start cutting the splint material so you do not waste time
choices.feedback: Too early. If you splint a hand that is already numb and never documented it, you own that finding. Baseline first, materials second.

choices.text: Ask her to make a tight fist to test the wrist
choices.feedback: Harmful. Making a fist moves the fracture and causes real pain. Motor testing means wiggling and spreading the fingers, not gripping.

choices.text: Remove her rings after checking the hand
choices.feedback: Reasonable and often necessary, since the hand will swell, but it comes after the neurovascular baseline, not instead of it.

steps.prompt: Radial pulse strong, capillary refill under `2 seconds`, fingers move and spread, sensation equal on both sides of every finger. You document it at 14:20. Which splint do you set up?

choices.text: Sugar-tong forearm splint
choices.feedback: Right. A distal radius fracture rotates, and only a splint crossing the elbow blocks supination and pronation.

choices.text: Volar forearm splint, since it is faster and more comfortable
choices.feedback: A common shortcut and it fails. A volar slab does not cross the elbow, so the fracture keeps rotating and can displace before follow-up.

choices.text: Thumb spica
choices.feedback: Wrong injury. Thumb spica is for a scaphoid fracture or suspicion and thumb ligament injuries, not the distal radius.

choices.text: Ask the provider to confirm sugar-tong versus long-arm before you build
choices.feedback: Never wrong to confirm, and it costs thirty seconds. Sugar-tong is the expected answer here, but checking an unclear order is good practice.

steps.prompt: You have OCL prepadded fiberglass, plaster, stockinette, Webril and elastic wraps on the cart. How do you measure and prepare?

choices.text: Measure the strip against her left arm, apply stockinette and 2-3 layers of Webril, then dip in warm water
choices.feedback: Exactly right. Measuring on the uninjured side avoids moving the fracture, and padding goes on before anything rigid.

choices.text: Measure on the injured arm so the fit is exact
choices.feedback: This means manipulating a fresh fracture for a measurement you can get from the other arm. It hurts and can displace the fracture.

choices.text: Skip the Webril, since the OCL is prepadded
choices.feedback: Tempting, but the ends and the bony points still need padding, and stockinette gives you something to fold back over the edges.

choices.text: Dip the plaster in hot water so it sets faster
choices.feedback: Dangerous. Hot water speeds the exothermic reaction and causes burns. Warm water, roughly 20-25 degrees C, is the standard.

steps.prompt: The material is on: palm side from the knuckles up the forearm, around the elbow at `90 degrees`, back down the dorsal side. Now you finish it. What do you do?

choices.text: Fold the stockinette back, wrap the elastic bandage distal to proximal, and mold with flat palms while it sets
choices.feedback: Correct on all three. Folding covers sharp edges, distal-to-proximal wrapping moves swelling toward the heart, and palms avoid divots that become pressure sores.

choices.text: Wrap the elastic bandage tightly from the elbow down to the hand
choices.feedback: Two errors. Wrapping toward the hand traps swelling there, and full tension turns the wrap into a tourniquet.

choices.text: Hold the mold with your fingertips to get a crisp contour at the wrist
choices.feedback: Fingertips leave divots in the curing material, and those become pressure points against the skin. Use flat palms.

choices.text: Wrap it and let her rest the arm on a pillow while it cures
choices.feedback: The wrap is fine, but a pillow under a curing splint insulates the exothermic reaction against her skin. Leave it exposed to air until it is set.

steps.prompt: The splint is firm. She is ready to go home with orthopedic follow-up in `5 days`. What do you do before she leaves?

choices.text: Recheck and document circulation, motor and sensation, then teach elevation, ice and the return precautions
choices.feedback: This is the whole job. The post-application check catches a wrap that is too tight, and the return precautions catch what happens after she leaves.

choices.text: Tell her to keep it dry and come back in five days
choices.feedback: Incomplete. She has no post-splint neurovascular check documented and no warning signs, which are the two things that protect her hand tonight.

choices.text: Tell her the numbness she now reports in two fingers should improve overnight
choices.feedback: Harmful. New numbness after splinting means the wrap is too tight. Loosen it now and tell the nurse or provider before she goes anywhere.

choices.text: Document the post-splint check but skip the warning signs to save time, since the discharge paperwork covers it
choices.feedback: Printed instructions get folded and forgotten. Say the three return precautions out loud: numbness, color or temperature change, and worsening pain.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: **check, choose, build, recheck, teach.** The neurovascular check brackets the splint on both ends, and it is the only way to prove the hand was fine before and to catch a wrap that is too tight after. The splint choice follows the mechanics of the fracture, not convenience: a distal radius fracture rotates, so the splint must cross the elbow, which is why the sugar-tong exists. The build details that seem cosmetic are the safety details: warm water and no insulation prevent burns, distal-to-proximal wrapping prevents a tourniquet, and palms instead of fingertips prevent pressure sores. Finally, she leaves knowing exactly what sends her back: numbness, pale or cold fingers, and pain that climbs instead of settling.

scenarios.title: Room 4: forearm laceration from a dirty utility knife
scenarios.intro: A 31-year-old man was breaking down cardboard in a warehouse when the utility knife slipped and cut the inside of his left forearm. It happened about `90 minutes` ago. The blade was greasy and had been used on boxes off a loading dock floor. He wrapped it in a shop towel. The provider has glanced at it and wants it irrigated and set up for repair. He is otherwise healthy and takes no medications.

steps.prompt: You unwrap the shop towel. There is a `6 cm` straight laceration on the volar forearm, edges gaping, oozing steadily, with visible grease and cardboard fibers in the base. What do you do first?

choices.text: Hold direct pressure with gauze, then describe and document the wound: 6 cm, depth, contamination, mechanism, time, and distal movement and sensation
choices.feedback: Correct. Control the bleeding, then build the description that drives every later decision, including whether it gets closed at all.

choices.text: Start irrigating immediately while it is still bleeding
choices.feedback: Irrigation is coming, but a wound that is actively oozing needs pressure first, and you have not yet documented distal function. A cut tendon or nerve found later looks very different if nobody checked before.

choices.text: Pack the wound with gauze and apply a pressure dressing until the provider returns
choices.feedback: This delays cleaning a contaminated wound for no reason. The infection clock is running and mechanical washing is the intervention that matters.

choices.text: Ask him to make a fist and extend each finger against your resistance, and check sensation past the wound
choices.feedback: Good instinct and part of the assessment, since a partly cut tendon still moves and only shows weakness against resistance. Do it as part of the documented description, after pressure controls the ooze.

steps.prompt: Bleeding is controlled. Fingers move fully against resistance and sensation is equal. The wound is `6 cm` and clearly dirty. How do you set up the irrigation?

choices.text: A 60 mL syringe with a splash guard, warm saline, about 600 mL, with a basin and pad under the arm and a face shield on
choices.feedback: Right on every count. That syringe and orifice gives 8-15 psi, 100 mL per centimeter means about 600 mL, and the shield keeps the splash out of your eyes.

choices.text: Pour a liter of saline slowly over the wound from the bottle
choices.feedback: Volume without pressure. Pouring is roughly 0.05 psi and leaves the bacteria and grease behind. It is the pressure that does the cleaning.

choices.text: Scrub the wound with a brush and dilute povidone-iodine
choices.feedback: Both halves are wrong. Scrubbing crushes tissue and raises infection rates, and iodine inside a wound kills the cells that heal it. Antiseptic goes on the skin around the wound.

choices.text: A 60 mL syringe with a splash guard, but only about 200 mL since he is uncomfortable
choices.feedback: Right equipment, not enough volume. A 6 cm contaminated wound needs roughly 600 mL. If he cannot tolerate it, that is an argument for anesthesia first, not for less irrigation.

steps.prompt: The wound is irrigated and looks clean. The provider will repair it. What do you put on the sterile tray?

choices.text: Needle driver, toothed forceps, suture scissors, gauze, fenestrated drape, a 10 mL syringe with a 25-27 gauge needle, and 4-0 nylon
choices.feedback: That is the standard laceration tray, and 4-0 is a reasonable forearm choice. Confirm the suture with the provider, but this is the right set.

choices.text: The same tray but with 6-0 nylon
choices.feedback: 6-0 is face suture. It is too fine to hold a 6 cm forearm wound that sits under tension when he bends his elbow, and it will pull through.

choices.text: Tissue adhesive and adhesive strips instead of a suture tray
choices.feedback: Wrong wound. Glue is for short, clean, low-tension lacerations with edges that meet on their own. This one is long, contaminated and gaping.

choices.text: The tray plus the lidocaine vial placed on the sterile field
choices.feedback: The instruments are right but the vial is not sterile on the outside. It stays off the field; someone holds it while the provider draws up.

steps.prompt: The provider asks you to check his tetanus history. He says he finished all his childhood shots and had a booster "maybe six or seven years ago, after a dog bite." What is the answer?

choices.text: He needs a Td or Tdap booster, because this is a dirty wound and it has been more than 5 years
choices.feedback: Correct. Dirty or deep wounds are boosted at over 5 years. The 10-year rule applies only to clean minor wounds.

choices.text: No booster needed, since it has been less than 10 years
choices.feedback: That applies the clean-wound rule to a dirty wound. Grease and floor contamination put this in the 5-year category.

choices.text: He needs a booster plus tetanus immune globulin
choices.feedback: Immune globulin is for patients with fewer than three lifetime doses or an unknown series. He completed his primary series, so vaccine alone is enough.

choices.text: Tell the provider the history is uncertain and let them decide
choices.feedback: Not wrong to escalate an unclear history, but you can reason this out: completed series plus a dirty wound plus more than 5 years equals a booster.

steps.prompt: The repair is done with `9` sutures. He asks what happens now and when the stitches come out. What do you tell him and what do you dress it with?

choices.text: Non-adherent dressing and dry gauze, first change at 24-48 hours, sutures out in 7-14 days, return for redness, spreading warmth, drainage or fever
choices.feedback: That is the complete discharge: dressing, change interval, removal window for an extremity, and specific infection warning signs for a wound that started dirty.

choices.text: Dry gauze and tape, sutures out in 3-5 days
choices.feedback: The dressing is acceptable but the timing is facial timing. A forearm needs 7-14 days, and over a joint 10-14, or the wound pulls open.

choices.text: Leave it open to air so it dries out, sutures out in 10 days
choices.feedback: The removal window is fine but wounds heal better covered and moist for the first day or two, and this one needs protection from the same warehouse environment that contaminated it.

choices.text: Tell him to soak the arm daily in hydrogen peroxide to keep it clean
choices.feedback: Harmful. Peroxide is toxic to healing tissue, and soaking a fresh sutured wound macerates it. Keep it clean and dry and follow the dressing plan.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern here is **describe, wash, set up, protect.** The description is not paperwork: mechanism, contamination and time since injury decide whether this wound is closed at all, and the distal motor and sensory exam is the only chance to catch a partly cut tendon before it is buried under sutures. Irrigation is the single intervention that changes infection rates, and it only works with both halves right, `8-15 psi` from a `35-60 mL` syringe with a splash guard and roughly `100 mL per centimeter` of wound. Nothing antiseptic goes inside. Tetanus splits on one number: `10` years for a clean minor wound, `5` years for anything dirty or deep, with immune globulin added only when the primary series is incomplete or unknown. Finally, removal timing follows the site, not the calendar in your head, and a wound that started dirty leaves with explicit infection warning signs.
